prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for B009, Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. I opened with B009 at rank six and moved to it only after the precision-measurement colleagues explained it, so I have tried in this round to test that move and not just repeat it. The reading I keep coming back to is a mechanism question. A magic wavelength makes the differential light shift between the clock states cancel, so a large ensemble can be held tightly without Doppler or recoil broadening and without perturbing the transition. That is a single, general idea that can be written down in a few lines and checked against experiment, which is how I judge theory-facing results. It has been realised and compared in independent laboratories with different species (Sr, Yb, Hg), and the agreement is itself the evidence that the physics is understood and not merely engineered. The consequences are also physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drift of constants, and strongly interacting many-body spin dynamics in the lattice. On exact credit, the two names carry separable roles that I would state in this way: Katori for the proposal and first demonstration of magic-wavelength trapping, Ye for taking the system to record accuracy and for the many-body understanding. I do not need the redefinition of the second to make the case, and I would keep it out of the citation, as Pearce argues.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks is still the principal reservation, and I have not been able to dismiss it by argument alone. The lattice clock uses the comb as readout and shares the clock-accuracy theme with the ion clocks. My view is that the overlap concerns infrastructure and goal, while the credited element, trapping and interrogating many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, is a different principle; but that is a judgement on a question where specialists could reasonably disagree. A second weakness is credit. Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Lemonde, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB and SYRTE groups made decisive contributions that a two-name prize leaves out, and I cannot verify the priority history myself. Third, whether no departure from known physics has been seen yet: this is a case of an extraordinary instrument whose largest scientific yield may still lie ahead, which is a weaker claim than a discovery of a new phenomenon. Finally, the apparent unanimity in round 1 is partly an artefact of five members moving after reading the same ballots, and I do not count it as evidence in itself.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B009 sixth in the opening, is less relaxed about the 2012 ion-clock prize than the 2005 comb prize, and wants the citation framed around the lattice concept and many-atom interrogation rather than clock accuracy in general.
responses.response: I share your ordering of the two precedents and agree on the framing. The 2005 prize honoured spectroscopy and the comb, which here is a tool. The 2012 prize is closer because it also concerns a clock, so the citation must name the new element: confinement of many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, which the ion-trap work does not cover. Your point that the lattice clock is not merely a reference but a many-body system is the argument that moves me most toward counting this as physics and not metrology alone. I would therefore drop accuracy figures from the citation and keep the principle. Since you and I both ranked it sixth in the opening and both came here by the same route, I would add that neither of us can judge the priority history, and we should ask experts.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether Ye's decisive contribution is the lattice clock itself or the wider JILA programme, and says the redefinition of the second is a consequence and not part of the discovery.
responses.response: I agree on the redefinition: it depends on decisions of metrology bodies and could slip, so it should not appear in the citation or carry weight in our judgement. On Ye I do not think the question has to be answered by the credit being less than the two names. The strontium lattice clock at JILA is the system in which the 1e-18 regime, the clock comparisons and the many-body spin physics were all reached, so his work is a realisation and understanding of the lattice clock and not only a neighbouring programme. What I cannot judge is how Hall's earlier role affects the framing, and I would accept an expert check on whether Ye's priority claims on specific milestones stand. If the expert reading narrowed his share, I would still prefer to keep two names over a single laureate, but I would want the check before the ballot.

responses.point: Danielsson says a prize about better numbers risks looking incremental, but that the pending redefinition of the second makes the timing right.
responses.response: I agree with the first half of your concern and disagree with the second. A prize for better numbers would be a weak prize, which is why I want the citation to rest on the trapping principle. I do not accept the redefinition as a timing argument, since it has not happened. The timing case should rest on what has already occurred: multiple independent clocks agree at the 1e-18 level, redshift has been resolved at millimetre scale, and constants-drift bounds have been tightened. Those are completed results, and I think they are sufficient without the redefinition.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the redefinition and the new-physics searches count as realised or still prospective impact, and wants the priority history checked.
responses.response: I would treat them as separate. The tests of redshift and of constant drift have been done and are published, with null results at a stated level, so they count as realised. The redefinition and any detection of new physics are prospective, and I would not let either bear weight. On priority, I agree with your request, and I record that I am relying on memory and on colleagues. I accept Lindroth's statement that the magic-wavelength priority is not seriously contested as Katori's, but nothing on file independently checks it, so I would support the request for outside evaluation of the clock lineage before the final ballot.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, on balance, sees magic-wavelength lattice trapping as a distinct principle from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes; I judge yes, but I cannot settle it by argument.

Whether the two-name credit is defensible once the contributions of Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Lemonde, Hinkley, Bloom, PTB and SYRTE are weighed; I rely on colleagues and have not checked the priority record.
Whether Ye's share rests on the lattice clock specifically or on the wider JILA programme, and how Hall's 2005 role bears on it.

If B009 were set aside, B010 requires choosing three of four names from Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger, and B005 has only partial confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents; I have no reserve that is clean on both science and credit.
I am outside precision atomic physics, and my agreement may owe something to how the other members framed the case.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name for B009 (Katori, Ye) or my alternatives B010 (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger) and B005 (Toner, Ramaswamy, Vicsek); none is among my frequent co-authors. I am a Gothenburg physics colleague of Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson at Chalmers, an institutional fact that does not concern any candidate in my preferred configuration. I do not work in optical clocks or active matter groups, and no disclosure has changed since round 1.
